memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: "'All its fat shall be offered: the fat tail and the fat that covers the internal organs, both kidneys with the fat on them near the loins, and the long lobe of the liver, which is to be removed with the kidneys.'" - Lev 7:3-4 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
We have read this list before — in the fellowship offering, the offering of celebration. Now it appears in the guilt offering, brought by someone who has wronged his neighbour.

The same choice parts. The same careful removal. The same portion given to God.

That is worth noticing. God does not take a reduced offering from the person who has failed. He does not say, "Given the circumstances, bring Me less." The best still belongs to Him, even on the worst day.

There is something dignifying in that. God did not treat the guilty Israelite as a second-class worshipper who had forfeited the right to give anything valuable. He treated him as a worshipper.

Some of us struggle here. After failing, we feel we have lost the right to serve, to give, to lead worship, to pray for anyone else. We disqualify ourselves.

But Peter denied Christ three times and was restored, and then told to feed my sheep (Jn 21:17). David wrote his most-loved psalm after his worst sin, and prayed, Restore to me the joy of your salvation... then I will teach transgressors your ways (Ps 51:12-13).

Failure changes what you have to say. It does not end your usefulness to God.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. Have I disqualified myself from serving God because of a past failure?
2. Am I still bringing God my best, or have I downgraded what I offer Him?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Father, thank You that You still want my best even after I have failed. Restore me, and let me serve You again. Amen.
